cases.answer: Liu et al. targeted GGGGCC-repeat RNA with Cas13d. Compared with non-targeting NT30, S24/S30 reduced poly-GP and poly-GA by approximately 20–90% across C9-ALS patient-derived motor-neuron lines, measured 10 days after lentiviral treatment. In C9-500 BAC mice injected with AAV9 at birth and examined at 13 months, treatment reduced poly-GP, poly-GA and poly-GA inclusions. These were molecular/pathological endpoints: repeat-RNA cleavage was limited and variable, RNA foci were not significantly reduced, and the mouse model lacked survival or motor deficits, leaving protective effects unestablished. Sachdeva et al. (the article corresponding to 'Sachdev') edited DNA in iPSCs and studied their differentiated motor neurons. Repeat-expansion excision or selective mutant-allele excision corrected RNA abnormalities, eliminated DPR production, preserved normal C9orf72 protein levels, reduced TDP-43 pathology and improved electrophysiological function. DPRs were measured at 2 weeks and TDP-43 at 7 weeks; residual nuclear TDP-43 loss remained despite the abstract's broader statement that excision reverted 'all pathology.' Its major limitation was reliance primarily on one patient cell line, with replication and further preclinical testing still required. Neither study establishes a human treatment: Liu demonstrates biomarker suppression in cells and mice with protective effects requiring further evaluation; Sachdeva demonstrates cellular proof of concept and explicitly proposes further testing in postmitotic neurons and animal models.

despite

claims.claim: The DNA-editing study manipulated human iPSCs and examined derived motor neurons as cellular proof of concept.
claims.quote:
We carried out these manipulations in human iPSCs and exam-
ined their impact on both the RNA and protein products of the 
C9orf72 locus, and on a cellular marker of C9/ALS pathology, 
TDP43, in motor neurons derived from the iPSCs.

claims.claim: Repeat or selective mutant-allele excision preserved protein levels, corrected RNA abnormalities, eliminated DPR production, reduced TDP-43 pathology and improved electrophysiological function.
claims.quote:
our two other approaches (biallelic excision of the repeat 
expansion, or selective excision of the mutant allele) preserved 
WT protein levels, corrected RNA abnormalities, abrogated 
dipeptide repeat production, reduced TDP43 pathology, and 
improved adaptive electrophysiologic function in patient- derived 
iPSC- derived motor neurons.

claims.claim: DPRs were assessed in 2-week-old neurons.
claims.quote:
Using these two combinations, we measured poly- GA 
and poly- GP DPRs in 2- wk- old neurons derived from our 
C9- isogenic series.

claims.claim: TDP-43 pathology was assessed at 7 weeks and was reduced rather than completely eliminated.
claims.quote:
at 7 
wk postinduction. We found that on average, less than 30% of the

claims.quote:
Excision of the mutant repeat expansion reverted

claims.claim: The DNA-editing findings primarily came from one patient cell line and require replication.
claims.quote:
A limitation of this study is that our biological

claims.claim: The DNA-editing approaches remain candidates for further preclinical testing.
claims.quote:

other_candidates.why_rejected: These are cited earlier studies; their mouse results are not animal-treatment results from Sachdeva et al.'s current study.

cases.ambiguity: The batch names Sachdev; the matching 2024 DNA-excision article lists Aradhana Sachdeva. The answer treats this as the intended study.

cases.answer: In the 42-year-old man's case, clinical progression and family history sustained suspicion despite imaging: CT was normal, MRI showed moderately dilated ventricles without a specific atrophy pattern, and SPECT was interpreted as most consistent with Alzheimer's disease rather than FTLD. Progressive cognitive and functional decline, atypical psychiatric symptoms and treatment non-response supported further investigation. His father had bulbar ALS diagnosed at 54 and died within 18 months, raising suspicion of a genetic FTD-ALS disorder. Genetic testing identified a GGGGCC repeat expansion in C9orf72, which the authors described as confirming FTD-ALS. Subsequent post-mortem examination confirmed frontotemporal lobar degeneration with TDP pathology, international harmonized classification type C.

A 42-year-old previously healthy male with a remote
